evidence_quotes.quote: This is an empirical case study of ‘street-level’ officials in a classic ‘regulatory’ public agency: the Environmental Health Department in Kumasi and Accra, Ghana, where privatisation and contracting-out of sanitary services have imposed new ways of working on Environmental Health Officers. Both internal and external organisational relationships are analysed to explain the extent to which these officers have adapted to more ‘client-oriented’ ways of working.

First, consequent upon their closer integration with Waste Management Departments, the EHOs are now expected to help supervise and monitor the performance of the new ‘franchised’ (private) waste collection and cleansing companies doing city-wide collections, latrine and septic tank emptying companies and managers of sanitary facilities.

The data on the front-line EHOs and their organisation were collected using a combination of participant observation (accompanying officers on their daily rounds), elite interviews and a questionnaire survey of 85 officers (virtually the total workforce) in four selected Sub-Metropolitan Districts (SMDs) of Accra and Kumasi.

In this study, we set out to explore and test a range of possible determinants of the changes which did (or did not) occur in the performance of the Environmental Health service, in particular the extent to which they understood and put into practice the new approaches.

Our linked random sample survey of 1,000 public toilet users in Accra, Kumasi and Sunyani revealed that 88% of citizens rated the cleanliness of gutters and drains in their neighbourhoods as ‘bad or very bad’, and 77% had a similar view of the quality of waste collection.

criterion_notes.c1: No. Although situated in the urban environmental sanitation sector (solid waste collection, storm drainage, food hygiene, pan-latrine emptying, and contracted public toilets) in Kumasi and Accra, the paper studies how front-line Environmental Health Officers (EHOs) adapt to organisational change rather than household or community access to water or sanitation services.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: YES — the paper examines institutional, administrative, and regulatory governance factors, including decentralisation of Environmental Health Officers to Metropolitan Assemblies, public-private partnership contracting-out/franchising of waste and public toilet management, internal agency management/organisational culture, and street-level regulatory enforcement. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: NO — the factors analysed (internal team solidarity, management style, staff training/morale, community clean-up animation, and nuisance/cleanliness compliance monitoring) do not constitute a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility criteria, tenure/documentation rules, tariffs/cost-recovery rules, or connection/disconnection rules). Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study is still excluded (plain_criterion2_decision = exclude) because it fails Criteria 1 and 4 by studying bureaucratic adaptation and neighbourhood cleanliness perceptions rather than water or sanitation service access outcomes.
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. Mixed-methods empirical case study combining a questionnaire survey of 85 front-line Environmental Health Officers across four Sub-Metropolitan Districts in Accra and Kumasi, participant observation on daily rounds, elite interviews, and summary findings from a linked random sample survey of 1,000 public toilet users.
criterion_notes.c4: No. Reported empirical outcomes are EHOs' attitudes toward client-oriented public education roles, job satisfaction, turnover intentions, perceptions of public friendliness and staff appraisals, constraints on prosecuting nuisances or sanctioning politically connected contractors, and public ratings of gutter/drain cleanliness, solid waste collection quality, and overall EHO impact on neighbourhood cleanliness. No water or sanitation service access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion outcome is reported.
criterion_notes.c5: Yes. The study design (mixed-methods empirical case study with officer survey, participant observation, and elite interviews), unit of analysis and sample (85 EHOs in four SMDs of Accra and Kumasi, plus 1,000 surveyed public toilet users), organisational/policy exposures, and bureaucratic/cleanliness outcomes are clearly identifiable, allowing confirmation that the outcome is out of scope.

study_design: Mixed-methods empirical case study (structured questionnaire survey of 85 officials, participant observation, elite interviews, and supplementary user perception survey)
population_and_sample: 85 front-line Environmental Health Officers (virtually the total workforce) in four Sub-Metropolitan Districts of Accra (Ayawaso, Kpeshie) and Kumasi (Asokwa, Subin), supplemented by a linked survey of 1,000 public toilet users in Accra, Kumasi, and Sunyani
exposure: Decentralisation of Environmental Health Officers to municipal governments, contracting-out/franchising of waste and sanitary services, internal organisational culture and management style, and local political patronage interfering with regulatory enforcement
outcome: Street-level bureaucrats' adaptation to client-oriented roles, job satisfaction, turnover intention, attitudes toward public education vs. regulatory enforcement, and citizen perceptions of gutter/drain cleanliness, waste collection quality, and EHO impact on neighbourhood cleanliness
rationale: Excluded (E04 - Wrong outcome; also fails C1 and narrow C2). This public-administration empirical case study examines how 85 street-level Environmental Health Officers in Accra and Kumasi, Ghana adapt to decentralisation, contracting-out of waste/sanitary services, and participatory public-health promotion, focusing on internal organisational culture, job satisfaction, attitudes toward citizens and contractors, and political interference with nuisance/contractor compliance enforcement. Neither the main officer survey nor the supplementary survey ratings of gutter/drain cleanliness and solid waste collection measure household or community sanitation service access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion, and the organisational factors studied do not operate as rule-type mechanisms directly governing service access.
